text: And that’s the difference between the president and me.

speaker: KERRY
text: And there, again, he sort of slid by the question.

speaker: KERRY
text: Now, with respect to Darfur, yes, it is a genocide.

speaker: KERRY
text: And months ago, many of us were pressing for action.

speaker: KERRY
text: I think the reason that we’re not saying send American troops in at this point is severalfold.

speaker: KERRY
text: Number one, we can do this through the African Union, providing we give them the logistical support.

speaker: KERRY
text: Right now all the president is providing is humanitarian support.

speaker: KERRY
text: We need to do more than that.

speaker: KERRY
text: They’ve got to have the logistical capacity to go in and stop the killing.

speaker: KERRY
text: And that’s going to require more than is on the table today.

speaker: KERRY
text: I also believe that it is — one of the reasons we can’t do it is we’re overextended.

speaker: KERRY
text: Ask the people in the armed forces today.

speaker: KERRY
text: We’ve got Guards and Reserves who are doing double duties.

speaker: KERRY
text: We’ve got a backdoor draft taking place in America today: people with stop-loss programs where they’re told you can’t get out of the military; nine out of our 10 active duty divisions committed to Iraq one way or the other, either going, coming or preparing.

speaker: KERRY
text: So this is the way the president has overextended the United States.

speaker: KERRY
text: That’s why, in my plan, I add two active duty divisions to the United States Army, not for Iraq, but for our general demands across the globe.

speaker: KERRY
text: I also intend to double the number of special forces so that we can do the job we need to do with respect fighting the terrorists around the world.

speaker: KERRY
text: And if we do that, then we have the ability to be able to respond more rapidly.

speaker: KERRY
text: But I’ll tell you this, as president, if it took American forces to some degree to coalesce the African Union, I’d be prepared to do it because we could never allow another Rwanda.

speaker: KERRY
text: It’s a moral responsibility for us and the world.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Ninety seconds.

speaker: BUSH
text: Back to Iran, just for a second.

speaker: BUSH
text: It was not my administration that put the sanctions on Iran.

speaker: BUSH
text: That happened long before I arrived in Washington, D.

speaker: BUSH
text: In terms of Darfur, I agree it’s genocide.

speaker: BUSH
text: And Colin Powell so stated.

speaker: BUSH
text: We have committed $200 million worth of aid.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’re the leading donor in the world to help the suffering people there.

speaker: BUSH
text: We will commit more over time to help.

speaker: BUSH
text: We were very much involved at the U.

speaker: BUSH
text: on the sanction policy of the Bashir government in the Sudan.

speaker: BUSH
text: Prior to Darfur, Ambassador Jack Danforth had been negotiating a north-south agreement that we would have hoped would have brought peace to the Sudan.

speaker: BUSH
text: I agree with my opponent that we shouldn’t be committing troops.

speaker: BUSH
text: We ought to be working with the African Union to do so — precisely what we did in Liberia.

speaker: BUSH
text: We helped stabilize the situation with some troops, and when the African Union came, we moved them out.

speaker: BUSH
text: My hope is that the African Union moves rapidly to help save lives.

speaker: BUSH
text: And fortunately the rainy season will be ending shortly, which will make it easier to get aid there and help the long-suffering people there.

speaker: LEHRER
text: New question, President Bush.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Clearly, as we have heard, major policy differences between the two of you.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Are there also underlying character issues that you believe, that you believe are serious enough to deny Senator Kerry the job as commander in chief of the United States?

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s a loaded question.

speaker: BUSH
text: Well, first of all, I admire Senator Kerry’s service to our country.

speaker: BUSH
text: I admire the fact that he is a great dad.

speaker: BUSH
text: I appreciate the fact that his daughters have been so kind to my daughters in what has been a pretty hard experience for, I guess, young girls, seeing their dads out there campaigning.

speaker: BUSH
text: I admire the fact that he served for 20 years in the Senate.

speaker: BUSH
text: Although I’m not so sure I admire the record.

speaker: BUSH
text: I won’t hold it against him that he went to Yale.

speaker: BUSH
text: There’s nothing wrong with that.

speaker: BUSH
text: My concerns about the senator is that, in the course of this campaign, I’ve been listening very carefully to what he says, and he changes positions on the war in Iraq.

speaker: BUSH
text: He changes positions on something as fundamental as what you believe in your core, in your heart of hearts, is right in Iraq.

speaker: BUSH
text: You cannot lead if you send mixed messages.

speaker: BUSH
text: Mixed messages send the wrong signals to our troops.

speaker: BUSH
text: Mixed messages send the wrong signals to our allies.

speaker: BUSH
text: Mixed messages send the wrong signals to the Iraqi citizens.

speaker: BUSH
text: And that’s my biggest concern about my opponent.

speaker: BUSH
text: I admire his service.

speaker: BUSH
text: But I just know how this world works, and that in the councils of government, there must be certainty from the U.

speaker: BUSH
text: president.

speaker: BUSH
text: Of course, we change tactics when need to, but we never change our beliefs, the strategic beliefs that are necessary to protect this country in the world.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Ninety second response, Senator.

speaker: KERRY
text: Well, first of all, I appreciate enormously the personal comments the president just made.

speaker: KERRY
text: And I share them with him.

speaker: KERRY
text: I think only if you’re doing this — and he’s done it more than I have in terms of the presidency — can you begin to get a sense of what it means to your families.

speaker: KERRY
text: And it’s tough.

speaker: KERRY
text: And so I acknowledge that his daughters — I’ve watched them.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’ve chuckled a few times at some of their comments.

speaker: KERRY
text: And…

speaker: BUSH
text: I’m trying to put a leash on them.

speaker: KERRY
text: Well, I know.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’ve learned not to do that.

speaker: KERRY
text: And I have great respect and admiration for his wife.

speaker: KERRY
text: I think she’s a terrific person…

speaker: BUSH
text: Thank you.

speaker: KERRY
text: … and a great first lady.

speaker: KERRY
text: But we do have differences.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’m not going to talk about a difference of character.

speaker: KERRY
text: I don’t think that’s my job or my business.

speaker: KERRY
text: But let me talk about something that the president just sort of finished up with.

speaker: KERRY
text: Maybe someone would call it a character trait, maybe somebody wouldn’t.

speaker: KERRY
text: But this issue of certainty.

speaker: KERRY
text: It’s one thing to be certain, but you can be certain and be wrong.

speaker: KERRY
text: It’s another to be certain and be right, or to be certain and be moving in the right direction, or be certain about a principle and then learn new facts and take those new facts and put them to use in order to change and get your policy right.

speaker: KERRY
text: What I worry about with the president is that he’s not acknowledging what’s on the ground, he’s not acknowledging the realities of North Korea, he’s not acknowledging the truth of the science of stem-cell research or of global warming and other issues.

speaker: KERRY
text: And certainty sometimes can get you in trouble.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Thirty seconds.

speaker: BUSH
text: Well, I think — listen, I fully agree that one should shift tactics, and we will, in Iraq.

speaker: BUSH
text: Our commanders have got all the flexibility to do what is necessary to succeed.

speaker: BUSH
text: But what I won’t do is change my core values because of politics or because of pressure.

speaker: BUSH
text: And it is one of the things I’ve learned in the White House, is that there’s enormous pressure on the president, and he cannot wilt under that pressure.

speaker: BUSH
text: Otherwise, the world won’t be better off.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Thirty seconds.

speaker: KERRY
text: I have no intention of wilting.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’ve never wilted in my life.

speaker: KERRY
text: And I’ve never wavered in my life.

speaker: KERRY
text: I know exactly what we need to do in Iraq, and my position has been consistent: Saddam Hussein is a threat.

speaker: KERRY
text: He needed to be disarmed.

speaker: KERRY
text: We needed to go to the U.

speaker: KERRY
text: The president needed the authority to use force in order to be able to get him to do something, because he never did it without the threat of force.

speaker: KERRY
text: But we didn’t need to rush to war without a plan to win the peace.

speaker: LEHRER
text: New question, two minutes, Senator Kerry.

speaker: LEHRER
text: If you are elected president, what will you take to that office thinking is the single most serious threat to the national security to the United States?

speaker: KERRY
text: Nuclear proliferation.

speaker: KERRY
text: Nuclear proliferation.

speaker: KERRY
text: There’s some 600-plus tons of unsecured material still in the former Soviet Union and Russia.

speaker: KERRY
text: At the rate that the president is currently securing it, it’ll take 13 years to get it.

speaker: KERRY
text: I did a lot of work on this.

speaker: KERRY
text: I wrote a book about it several years ago — six, seven years ago — called “The New War,” which saw the difficulties of this international criminal network.

speaker: KERRY
text: And back then, we intercepted a suitcase in a Middle Eastern country with nuclear materials in it.

speaker: KERRY
text: And the black market sale price was about $250 million.

speaker: KERRY
text: Now, there are terrorists trying to get their hands on that stuff today.

speaker: KERRY
text: And this president, I regret to say, has secured less nuclear material in the last two years since 9/11 than we did in the two years preceding 9/11.

speaker: KERRY
text: We have to do this job.

speaker: KERRY
text: And to do the job, you can’t cut the money for it.

speaker: KERRY
text: The president actually cut the money for it.

speaker: KERRY
text: You have to put the money into it and the funding and the leadership.

speaker: KERRY
text: And part of that leadership is sending the right message to places like North Korea.

speaker: KERRY
text: Right now the president is spending hundreds of millions of dollars to research bunker-busting nuclear weapons.

speaker: KERRY
text: The United States is pursuing a new set of nuclear weapons.

speaker: KERRY
text: It doesn’t make sense.

speaker: KERRY
text: You talk about mixed messages.

speaker: KERRY
text: We’re telling other people, “You can’t have nuclear weapons,” but we’re pursuing a new nuclear weapon that we might even contemplate using.

speaker: KERRY
text: Not this president.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’m going to shut that program down, and we’re going to make it clear to the world we’re serious about containing nuclear proliferation.

speaker: KERRY
text: And we’re going to get the job of containing all of that nuclear material in Russia done in four years.

speaker: KERRY
text: And we’re going to build the strongest international network to prevent nuclear proliferation.

speaker: KERRY
text: This is the scale of what President Kennedy set out to do with the nuclear test ban treaty.

speaker: KERRY
text: It’s our generation’s equivalent.

speaker: KERRY
text: And I intend to get it done.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Ninety seconds, Mr.

speaker: LEHRER
text: President.

speaker: BUSH
text: Actually, we’ve increased funding for dealing with nuclear proliferation about 35 percent since I’ve been the president.

speaker: BUSH
text: Secondly, we’ve set up what’s called the — well, first of all, I agree with my opponent that the biggest threat facing this country is weapons of mass destruction in the hands of a terrorist network.

speaker: BUSH
text: And that’s why proliferation is one of the centerpieces of a multi-prong strategy to make the country safer.

speaker: BUSH
text: My administration started what’s called the Proliferation Security Initiative.

speaker: BUSH
text: Over 60 nations involved with disrupting the trans-shipment of information and/or weapons of mass destruction materials.

speaker: BUSH
text: And we’ve been effective.

speaker: BUSH
text: We busted the A.

speaker: BUSH
text: Khan network.

speaker: BUSH
text: This was a proliferator out of Pakistan that was selling secrets to places like North Korea and Libya.

speaker: BUSH
text: We convinced Libya to disarm.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s a central part of dealing with weapons of mass destruction and proliferation.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ll tell you another way to help protect America in the long run is to continue with missile defenses.

speaker: BUSH
text: And we’ve got a robust research and development program that has been ongoing during my administration.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ll be implementing a missile-defense system relatively quickly.

speaker: BUSH
text: And that is another way to help deal with the threats that we face in the 21st century.

speaker: BUSH
text: My opponent opposed the missile defenses.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Just for this one-minute discussion here, just for whatever seconds it takes: So it’s correct to say, that if somebody is listening to this, that both of you agree, if you’re reelected, Mr.

speaker: LEHRER
text: President, and if you are elected, the single most serious threat you believe, both of you believe, is nuclear proliferation?

speaker: BUSH
text: In the hands of a terrorist enemy.

speaker: KERRY
text: Weapons of mass destruction, nuclear proliferation.

speaker: KERRY
text: But again, the test or the difference between us, the president has had four years to try to do something about it, and North Korea has got more weapons; Iran is moving towards weapons.

speaker: KERRY
text: And at his pace, it will take 13 years to secure those weapons in Russia.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’m going to do it in four years, and I’m going to immediately set out to have bilateral talks with North Korea.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Your response to that?

speaker: BUSH
text: Again, I can’t tell you how big a mistake I think that is, to have bilateral talks with North Korea.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s precisely what Kim Jong Il wants.

speaker: BUSH
text: It will cause the six-party talks to evaporate.

speaker: BUSH
text: It will mean that China no longer is involved in convincing, along with us, for Kim Jong Il to get rid of his weapons.

speaker: BUSH
text: It’s a big mistake to do that.

speaker: BUSH
text: We must have China’s leverage on Kim Jong Il, besides ourselves.

speaker: BUSH
text: And if you enter bilateral talks, they’ll be happy to walk away from the table.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t think that’ll work.

speaker: LEHRER
text: All right.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Mr.

speaker: LEHRER
text: President, this is the last question.

speaker: LEHRER
text: And two minutes.

speaker: LEHRER
text: It’s a new subject — new question, and it has to do with President Putin and Russia.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Did you misjudge him or are you — do you feel that what he is doing in the name of antiterrorism by changing some democratic processes is OK?

speaker: BUSH
text: No, I don’t think it’s OK, and said so publicly.

speaker: BUSH
text: I think that there needs to be checks and balances in a democracy, and made that very clear that by consolidating power in the central government, he’s sending a signal to the Western world and United States that perhaps he doesn’t believe in checks and balances, and I told him that.

speaker: BUSH
text: I mean, he’s also a strong ally in the war on terror.

speaker: BUSH
text: He is — listen, they went through a horrible situation in Beslan, where these terrorists gunned down young school kids.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s the nature of the enemy, by the way.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s why we need to be firm and resolved in bringing them to justice.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s precisely what Vladimir Putin understands, as well.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ve got a good relation with Vladimir.

speaker: BUSH
text: And it’s important that we do have a good relation, because that enables me to better comment to him, and to better to discuss with him, some of the decisions he makes.

speaker: BUSH
text: I found that, in this world, that it’s important to establish good personal relationships with people so that when you have disagreements, you’re able to disagree in a way that is effective.

speaker: BUSH
text: And so I’ve told him my opinion.

speaker: BUSH
text: I look forward to discussing it more with him, as time goes on.

speaker: BUSH
text: Russia is a country in transition.

speaker: BUSH
text: Vladimir is going to have to make some hard choices.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I think it’s very important for the American president, as well as other Western leaders, to remind him of the great benefits of democracy, that democracy will best help the people realize their hopes and aspirations and dreams.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I will continue working with him over the next four years.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Ninety seconds, Senator Kerry.

speaker: KERRY
text: Well, let me just say quickly that I’ve had an extraordinary experience of watching up close and personal that transition in Russia, because I was there right after the transformation.

speaker: KERRY
text: And I was probably one of the first senators, along with Senator Bob Smith of New Hampshire, a former senator, to go down into the KGB underneath Treblinka Square and see reams of files with names in them.

speaker: KERRY
text: It sort of brought home the transition to democracy that Russia was trying to make.

speaker: KERRY
text: I regret what’s happened in these past months.

speaker: KERRY
text: And I think it goes beyond just the response to terror.

speaker: KERRY
text: Mr.

speaker: KERRY
text: Putin now controls all the television stations.

speaker: KERRY
text: His political opposition is being put in jail.

speaker: KERRY
text: And I think it’s very important to the United States, obviously, to have a working relationship that is good.

speaker: KERRY
text: This is a very important country to us.

speaker: KERRY
text: We want a partnership.

speaker: KERRY
text: But we always have to stand up for democracy.

speaker: KERRY
text: As George Will said the other day, “Freedom on the march; not in Russia right now.

speaker: KERRY
text: ” Now, I’d like to come back for a quick moment, if I can, to that issue about China and the talks.

speaker: KERRY
text: Because that’s one of the most critical issues here: North Korea.

speaker: KERRY
text: Just because the president says it can’t be done, that you’d lose China, doesn’t mean it can’t be done.

speaker: KERRY
text: I mean, this is the president who said “There were weapons of mass destruction,” said “Mission accomplished,” said we could fight the war on the cheap — none of which were true.

speaker: KERRY
text: We could have bilateral talks with Kim Jong Il.

speaker: KERRY
text: And we can get those weapons at the same time as we get China.

speaker: KERRY
text: Because China has an interest in the outcome, too.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Thirty seconds, Mr.

speaker: LEHRER
text: President.

speaker: BUSH
text: You know my opinion on North Korea.

speaker: BUSH
text: I can’t say it any more plainly.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Well, but when he used the word “truth” again…

speaker: BUSH
text: Pardon me?

speaker: LEHRER
text: … talking about the truth of the matter.

speaker: LEHRER
text: He used the word “truth” again.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Did that raise any hackles with you?

speaker: BUSH
text: Oh, I’m a pretty calm guy.

speaker: BUSH
text: I don’t take it personally.

speaker: LEHRER
text: OK.

speaker: LEHRER
text: All right.

speaker: BUSH
text: You know, we looked at the same intelligence and came to the same conclusion: that Saddam Hussein was a grave threat.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I don’t hold it against him that he said grave threat.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’m not going to go around the country saying he didn’t tell the truth, when he looked at the same intelligence I did.

speaker: KERRY
text: It was a threat.

speaker: KERRY
text: That’s not the issue.

speaker: KERRY
text: The issue is what you do about it.

speaker: KERRY
text: The president said he was going to build a true coalition, exhaust the remedies of the U.

speaker: KERRY
text: and go to war as a last resort.

speaker: KERRY
text: Those words really have to mean something.

speaker: KERRY
text: And, unfortunately, he didn’t go to war as a last resort.

speaker: KERRY
text: Now we have this incredible mess in Iraq — $200 billion.

speaker: KERRY
text: It’s not what the American people thought they were getting when they voted.

speaker: LEHRER
text: All right, that brings us to closing statements.

speaker: LEHRER
text: And, again, as determined by a coin toss, Senator Kerry, you go first, and you have two minutes.

speaker: KERRY
text: Thank you, Jim, very much.

speaker: KERRY
text: Thank you very much to the university, again.

speaker: KERRY
text: Thank you, Mr.

speaker: KERRY
text: President.

speaker: KERRY
text: My fellow Americans, as I’ve said at the very beginning of this debate, both President Bush and I love this country very much.

speaker: KERRY
text: There’s no doubt, I think, about that.

speaker: KERRY
text: But we have a different set of convictions about how we make our country stronger here at home and respected again in the world.

speaker: KERRY
text: I know that for many of you sitting at home, parents of kids in Iraq, you want to know who’s the person who could be a commander in chief who could get your kids home and get the job done and win the peace.

speaker: KERRY
text: And for all the rest of the parents in America who are wondering about their kids going to the school or anywhere else in the world, what kind of world they’re going to grow up in, let me look you in the eye and say to you: I defended this country as a young man in war, and I will defend it as president of the United States.

speaker: KERRY
text: But I have a difference with this president.

speaker: KERRY
text: I believe when we’re strongest when we reach out and lead the world and build strong alliances.

speaker: KERRY
text: I have a plan for Iraq.

speaker: KERRY
text: I believe we can be successful.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’m not talking about leaving.

speaker: KERRY
text: I’m talking about winning.

speaker: KERRY
text: And we need a fresh start, a new credibility, a president who can bring allies to our side.

speaker: KERRY
text: I also have a plan to win the war on terror, funding homeland security, strengthening our military, cutting our finances, reaching out to the world, again building strong alliances.

speaker: KERRY
text: I believe America’s best days are ahead of us because I believe that the future belongs to freedom, not to fear.

speaker: KERRY
text: That’s the country that I’m going to fight for.

speaker: KERRY
text: And I ask you to give me the opportunity to make you proud.

speaker: KERRY
text: I ask you to give me the opportunity to lead this great nation, so that we can be stronger here at home, respected again in the world, and have responsible leadership that we deserve.

speaker: KERRY
text: Thank you.

speaker: KERRY
text: And God bless America.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Mr.

speaker: LEHRER
text: President, two minutes.

speaker: BUSH
text: Thank you very much tonight, Jim.

speaker: BUSH
text: Senator.

speaker: BUSH
text: If America shows uncertainty or weakness in this decade, the world will drift toward tragedy.

speaker: BUSH
text: That’s not going to happen, so long as I’m your president.

speaker: BUSH
text: The next four years we will continue to strengthen our homeland defenses.

speaker: BUSH
text: We will strengthen our intelligence-gathering services.

speaker: BUSH
text: We will reform our military.

speaker: BUSH
text: The military will be an all-volunteer army.

speaker: BUSH
text: We will continue to stay on the offense.

speaker: BUSH
text: We will fight the terrorists around the world so we do not have to face them here at home.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ll continue to build our alliances.

speaker: BUSH
text: I’ll never turn over America’s national security needs to leaders of other countries, as we continue to build those alliances.

speaker: BUSH
text: And we’ll continue to spread freedom.

speaker: BUSH
text: I believe in the transformational power of liberty.

speaker: BUSH
text: I believe that the free Iraq is in this nation’s interests.

speaker: BUSH
text: I believe a free Afghanistan is in this nation’s interest.

speaker: BUSH
text: And I believe both a free Afghanistan and a free Iraq will serve as a powerful example for millions who plead in silence for liberty in the broader Middle East.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ve done a lot of hard work together over the last three and a half years.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ve been challenged, and we’ve risen to those challenges.

speaker: BUSH
text: We’ve climbed the mighty mountain.

speaker: BUSH
text: I see the valley below, and it’s a valley of peace.

speaker: BUSH
text: By being steadfast and resolute and strong, by keeping our word, by supporting our troops, we can achieve the peace we all want.

speaker: BUSH
text: I appreciate your listening tonight.

speaker: BUSH
text: I ask for your vote.

speaker: BUSH
text: And may God continue to bless our great land.

speaker: LEHRER
text: And that ends tonight’s debate.

speaker: LEHRER
text: A reminder, the second presidential debate will be a week from tomorrow, October 8th, from Washington University in St.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Louis.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Charles Gibson of ABC News will moderate a town hall-type event.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Then, on October 13th, from Arizona State University in Tempe, Bob Schieffer of CBS News will moderate an exchange on domestic policy that will be similar in format to tonight’s.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Also, this coming Tuesday, at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, the vice presidential candidates, Vice President Cheney and Senator Edwards, will debate with my PBS colleague, Gwen Ifill, moderating.

speaker: LEHRER
text: For now, thank you, Senator Kerry, President Bush.

speaker: LEHRER
text: From Coral Gables, Florida, I’m Jim Lehrer.

speaker: LEHRER
text: Thank you and good night.
